title: Read replicas
description: Read replicas are copies of the data that serve reads while the primary handles writes — the simplest way to scale read throughput. Replication lag means a replica can serve slightly stale data; applications that need read-your-writes route those reads to the primary. Adding replicas scales reads linearly until the primary's write fan-out becomes the bottleneck.
mechanism: Primary streams its write-ahead log to replicas, which replay it in order. Health checks remove lagging replicas from the read pool. Failover promotes a replica when the primary dies.
algo: Read capacity scales ~O(replicas). Lag is the log-ship + replay delay, usually milliseconds to seconds.

title: Eventual consistency
description: Eventual consistency promises that if writes stop, all replicas converge to the same value — without promising when. It trades immediate agreement for availability and speed: every replica accepts writes locally, and background anti-entropy reconciles differences. Most edge systems choose it because the alternative (waiting for a quorum across continents) is hundreds of milliseconds per write.
mechanism: Local writes + asynchronous propagation (gossip, log shipping). Anti-entropy: replicas compare Merkle trees of their data and exchange only differing ranges. Convergence is guaranteed if the network eventually delivers.
algo: Write latency is local: O(1). Convergence time depends on the anti-entropy interval and network — typically seconds.
complexity: O(1) local writes; convergence in seconds

title: Vector clocks
description: Vector clocks track causality across replicas: each replica keeps a counter per node, and comparing two clocks tells you whether one write happened before the other or they are concurrent. Concurrent writes are the conflicts that need resolution; causal ones are not. They are the standard alternative to wall-clock timestamps, which lie across machines.
mechanism: Clock = {node: counter}. On local write, increment own counter. On receiving a write, take element-wise max. Clock A < B iff every counter in A <= B and some <. Incomparable clocks = concurrent = conflict.
algo: O(nodes) per compare and merge. Clock size grows with node count — the main practical drawback.
demo:
def inc(clock, node):
    clock[node] = clock.get(node, 0) + 1
    return clock

def compare(a, b):
    nodes = set(a) | set(b)
    le = all(a.get(n, 0) <= b.get(n, 0) for n in nodes)
    ge = all(a.get(n, 0) >= b.get(n, 0) for n in nodes)
    if le and not ge:
        return 'a happened-before b'
    if ge and not le:
        return 'b happened-before a'
    return 'CONCURRENT (conflict!)'

a = inc({'n1': 1}, 'n1')          # n1 writes twice
b = inc({'n1': 1}, 'n2')          # n2 writes without seeing n1's second write
print('clock a:', a, '| clock b:', b)
print('relation:', compare(a, b))

title: Gossip protocols
description: Gossip spreads information like a rumor: each node periodically picks a random peer and exchanges state. Coverage grows exponentially — a message reaches all N nodes in about log(N) rounds — and no coordinator is needed. It is how cluster membership, failure detection, and anti-entropy all work at scale: simple, robust, and self-healing when nodes join or leave.
mechanism: Every T seconds, each node picks k random peers and sends its digest (version vectors, membership list). Peers reply with what they are missing. Infected nodes infect others; the classic analysis shows O(log N) rounds to full coverage.
algo: O(log N) rounds to converge; O(1) messages per node per round. Redundant messages are the cost of robustness.
demo:
import random
random.seed(2)
N = 16
infected = {0}
rounds = 0
while len(infected) < N:
    rounds += 1
    new = set()
    for n in list(infected):
        peer = random.randrange(N)  # pick a random peer, tell them the rumor
        new.add(peer)
    infected |= new
    print('round %d: %d/%d know' % (rounds, len(infected), N))
print('full coverage in ~log2(%d) rounds, no coordinator' % N)

title: CRDTs
description: Conflict-free replicated data types are data structures whose concurrent updates always merge to the same result, no coordination needed: G-Counters only increment, OR-Sets track adds with unique tags, LWW-Registers pick the latest timestamp. Two replicas that receive the same updates in different orders converge identically. They are the mathematical answer to edge replication conflicts.
mechanism: State-based: merge = join (least upper bound) of the two states, commutative/associative/idempotent. Op-based: operations commute. G-Counter merge takes element-wise max; OR-Set merge unions add-tags minus remove-tags.
algo: Merge is O(state size); G-Counter is O(nodes). Convergence is guaranteed by the lattice properties, not by protocol.

title: CDN edge caching
description: CDNs replicate content to hundreds of edge points of presence so users fetch from nearby instead of across the world. The edge caches by URL with cache-control headers; a miss goes to the origin (or a parent shield) and populates the edge. Purging propagates invalidation globally in seconds. The result: static content served in tens of milliseconds worldwide.
mechanism: Anycast DNS routes users to the nearest PoP; PoP checks its cache, then the regional shield, then origin. Surrogate keys allow purging groups of URLs at once. Stale-while-revalidate keeps serving during origin slowness.
algo: Edge hit is O(1) local. Purge propagation is O(PoPs) fan-out, typically seconds globally.

title: Conflict resolution strategies
description: When concurrent writes collide, something must decide the winner: last-write-wins (highest timestamp), application merge (union the sets), or user intervention (show both, let a human pick). LWW is simple and total but silently drops data; CRDT merges preserve everything but only work for compatible types; human resolution is correct but does not scale. The strategy is chosen per data type, not per system.
mechanism: Detect via vector clocks or version vectors; classify (causal = no conflict, concurrent = resolve). Apply the per-type resolver: LWW register, OR-Set union, or queue for manual review with both versions preserved.
algo: Detection O(nodes); resolution O(value) for merges, O(1) for LWW. Manual queues grow with conflict rate.
demo:
# concurrent writes to a shopping cart: LWW drops data, set-union merge keeps it
w1 = {'items': {'apple'}, 'ts': 10}
w2 = {'items': {'banana'}, 'ts': 12}  # concurrent: neither saw the other

lww = w1 if w1['ts'] > w2['ts'] else w2
print('last-write-wins:', lww['items'], '(apple silently lost!)')
merged = {'items': w1['items'] | w2['items']}
print('set-union merge :', merged['items'], '(nothing lost; right for add-only data)')
print('rule: pick the resolver per data type, not per system')

title: Write forwarding vs local writes
description: Multi-region systems choose where writes go: forwarding sends every write to the primary region (simple, consistent, slow for distant users), while local writes accept everywhere and reconcile later (fast, needs conflict handling). Active-active databases take local writes with CRDTs; classic primary-replica setups forward. The latency difference is a full inter-region round trip per write.
mechanism: Forwarding: edge proxies the write to the primary and waits. Local: edge applies to the local replica, returns, and replicates asynchronously with vector-clock conflict detection.
algo: Forwarded write latency = inter-region RTT + primary write. Local write latency = local write only; reconciliation is background.
demo:
RTT = 120  # ms inter-region

def forwarded_write():
    return RTT + 5  # proxy to primary, wait, ack

def local_write():
    return 5  # apply locally, replicate in background

print('forwarded write latency: %d ms (user waits for another continent)' % forwarded_write())
print('local write latency    : %d ms (reconcile later with vector clocks)' % local_write())
print('trade: consistency-now vs speed-now')

title: Geo-routing
description: Geo-routing sends each user to the nearest healthy region using DNS anycast, latency-based routing, or explicit geolocation. Health checks remove sick regions in seconds; traffic shifts automatically. The subtle part is stickiness: some applications need the same user to hit the same region (for session locality), so routers hash the user id consistently across regions.
mechanism: Route53-style latency records or anycast BGP; health checker per region; consistent hash on user id for stickiness within the healthy set. Failover = health check fails -> DNS/anycast withdraws the region.
algo: O(1) routing decision per request. Failover time = health-check interval x threshold, typically 10-30s.

title: Replication lag monitoring
description: Replication lag is the delay between a write committing on the primary and appearing on a replica — the staleness budget made visible. Monitoring tracks it per replica with heartbeats (write a timestamped marker, measure when each replica applies it). Alerts fire when lag exceeds the SLO; automation removes chronically lagging replicas from the read pool before users notice.
mechanism: Heartbeat table updated every second on the primary; replicas report the newest heartbeat they have applied; lag = now - heartbeat_ts. Expose per-replica lag as a gauge; page when p99 lag > threshold.
algo: O(replicas) heartbeat checks per interval. Lag SLO typically seconds; minutes means something is broken.
demo:
import time

primary_ts = [1000]
replica_applied = [1000, 998]  # replica 1 is 2s behind
SLO = 5

def check():
    now = 1005
    for i, applied in enumerate(replica_applied):
        lag = now - applied
        status = 'OK' if lag <= SLO else 'ALERT: remove from read pool'
        print('replica %d lag=%ds -> %s' % (i, lag, status))

check()
print('heartbeat markers make lag measurable; SLO breach -> automated removal')

title: Split-brain handling
description: Split-brain is when a network partition leaves two sides each thinking it is the authority — both accepting writes, diverging. Prevention beats cure: quorums (majority required for writes) mean only one side can proceed. When it happens anyway, recovery reconciles with vector clocks, keeps both histories, and resolves per the data type's merge rules. Never silently pick a winner and drop the other side's writes.
mechanism: Quorum writes (W > N/2) guarantee at most one writable side. Fencing tokens prevent a deposed primary from writing. On heal: exchange version vectors, identify divergent keys, merge per-type.
algo: Quorum check is O(1) per write. Divergence detection on heal is O(keys) version-vector compare.
demo:
# 5 nodes split 3|2: only the majority side accepts writes (quorum W=3)
nodes = {'a': 1, 'b': 1, 'c': 1, 'd': 0, 'e': 0}  # 1 = reachable
N, W = 5, 3

def can_write(side):
    return sum(nodes[n] for n in side) >= W

side1, side2 = ['a', 'b', 'c'], ['d', 'e']
print('side ABC (3 nodes) writable:', can_write(side1))
print('side DE  (2 nodes) writable:', can_write(side2), '(minority: reads only)')
print('quorum guarantees at most one writable side: no split-brain writes')

title: Edge compute (workers at edge)
description: Edge compute runs code at the CDN edge — request routing, auth, A/B tests, even vector re-ranking — within milliseconds of the user. Workers are isolates (V8) that start in under 5ms, run per request, and access edge KV storage. The constraint is limits: CPU milliseconds, memory megabytes, no long-lived connections. Design for stateless handlers with cached state, not servers shrunk down.
mechanism: Request -> nearest PoP -> isolate spun up (or warm) -> handler runs with bindings (KV, env) -> response. State lives in edge KV/Durable Objects; compute stays stateless and short.
algo: Cold start ~5ms (isolates) vs ~100ms+ (containers). Per-request cost is bounded by CPU-time limits.
demo:
# edge worker: stateless handler, KV binding, runs near the user
KV = {'user:1:plan': 'pro', 'flag:new-ui': 'on'}  # edge KV, replicated to PoPs

def handle(request):
    user = request['user']
    plan = KV.get('user:%s:plan' % user, 'free')
    variant = KV.get('flag:new-ui')
    # personalize + A/B at the edge: no origin round trip
    return {'plan': plan, 'ui': variant, 'served_from': 'edge-pop-ewr'}

print(handle({'user': '1'}))
print('auth, flags, and personalization resolved in ~5ms at the edge')

title: Data residency
description: Data residency laws (GDPR, data localization) require certain data to stay inside a country or region — replication must respect borders, not just latency. Residency-aware placement pins tenants' data to allowed regions at the shard-map level; cross-border replication is disabled for those tenants, and even backups stay in-region. Violations are legal incidents, so the router treats region constraints as hard, not advisory.
mechanism: Tenant metadata carries allowed_regions; the placement engine only assigns replicas within the set; the router rejects cross-region reads for pinned tenants. Audit proves placement, not just policy.
algo: Placement constraint check is O(1) per assignment. The cost is operational: per-region capacity planning instead of global pooling.

title: Anti-entropy with Merkle trees
description: Anti-entropy keeps replicas converged without shipping all the data: each replica builds a Merkle tree over its key ranges, and replicas compare tree roots — equal roots mean equal data. Differences descend the tree to the exact differing key ranges, and only those ranges are exchanged. Dynamo pioneered it; every eventually-consistent store uses some variant.
mechanism: Hash each key range into leaves; internal nodes hash their children. Exchange roots; on mismatch, exchange children recursively until the differing leaves (key ranges) are found; ship only those ranges.
algo: Tree build is O(keys); compare is O(differing ranges * log ranges). Equal replicas exchange O(1) hashes.
complexity: O(1) when equal; O(diff log n) when not
demo:
import hashlib

def h(x):
    return hashlib.md5(str(x).encode()).hexdigest()[:8]

def merkle(keys):
    leaves = sorted(h(k) for k in keys)
    while len(leaves) > 1:
        leaves = [h(leaves[i] + leaves[i+1]) if i + 1 < len(leaves) else leaves[i]
                  for i in range(0, len(leaves), 2)]
    return leaves[0]

rep_a = ['k1', 'k2', 'k3']
rep_b = ['k1', 'k2', 'k3-changed']
print('root A:', merkle(rep_a))
print('root B:', merkle(rep_b))
print('roots differ -> descend tree, exchange only the differing range (not all keys)')

title: Edge replication topologies
description: Replication topology shapes latency and resilience: star (all edges sync from one hub — simple, hub is a bottleneck), tree (hierarchical fan-out — scales, slower convergence), mesh (peer gossip — robust, chattiest), and ring. Edge networks usually run hub-and-spoke per region with gossip between hubs: fast local convergence, bounded cross-region chatter.
mechanism: Choose per link type: hub sync for bulk data within a region, gossip between regional hubs for metadata. Topology is configuration, re-evaluated as region count grows.
algo: Star converges in O(1) hops through the hub; gossip mesh in O(log N) rounds; tree in O(depth).
demo:
# rounds for an update to reach all 64 edge PoPs under each topology
import math
N = 64
print('star : 2 hops (edge->hub->edge), hub is the bottleneck')
print('tree : %d hops (fan-out 4)' % math.ceil(math.log(N, 4)))
print('mesh : ~%d gossip rounds (robust, chattiest)' % math.ceil(math.log2(N)))
print('practice: hub-and-spoke per region + gossip between regional hubs')
